This work extends the equivalents introduced in [1] for multiuser powerline communication (PLC) and radio frequency (RF) systems to open-access (public) RF systems for both existing SISO-OFDM users and new MISO-OFDM users, represented as vertical multiantenna users. These equivalents transform the multidimensional (OFDM) problem into a single-dimensional one and convert diagonal (no cross-linking between subcarriers) links into multiple cross-linking "generic" links. While the specific technique for achieving this diagonal-to-generic conversion differs between SISO and MISO configurations, the resulting equivalents maintain identical statistical properties, enabling the application of any multiuser access scheme across all subcarriers in the OFDM domain. Consequently, one or multiple datastreams per subcarrier can be transmitted using techniques such as time division multiple access (TDMA), code division multiple access (CDMA), or even multiple input multiple output (MIMO) approaches. To illustrate the utility of these equivalents, we adapt a prior result from the PLC domain regarding optimal access schemes for single-user point-to-point links with known integer-space channel distributions [2]. We demonstrate that this result holds true for both public SISO and MISO OFDM systems. Furthermore, we utilize these equivalents to analyze a simple point-to-point public RF system, comparing the performance of the conventional OFDM scheme against the equivalent's point-to-point generic system. Our findings indicate that while OFDM generally underperforms point-to-point solutions in single-user public scenarios, its advantages become significant in multiuser environments. Finally, we apply the OFDM and point-to-point generic equivalents to a multiuser system to evaluate their performance.

Nonlocal gravity theories offer promising frameworks for exploring nonlocal gravitational effects and addressing fundamental issues in theoretical physics, including quantum gravity and unified theories. In constitutive nonlocal gravitation, the nonlocality of the constitutive tensor enables the tensor itself to become nonlocal, while the fundamental tensor remains local. Unlike metric-based nonlocal gravitation models, constitutive approaches allow for a local fundamental tensor that does not need to be metric-compatible, opening up nonmetric-based theories. This paper introduces a nonlocal constitutive tensor in a Spangler-Feynman-type framework, defining a nonlocal Levi-Civita tensor based on the local metric and a nonlocal Christoffel symbol derived from the local metric and a local nonlocal constitutive connection. We establish the representation of this nonlocal connection as a sum of a local Einstein-Cartan connection and a nonlocal Papapetrou tensor, which in turn determines the nonlocal Riemann tensor. Additionally, we formulate a nonlocal curvature tensor and an additional nonlocal curvature tensor, which is traceless and anharmonic. We explicitly express this additional nonlocal curvature tensor as a function of the nonlocal Riemann tensor and the nonlocal constitutive tensor, and we extend this formulation to the nonlocal Weyl tensor. Future work will involve developing a action for nonlocal gravitation and investigating its physical implications. This research constitutes work by a single author. An open-source Python package implementing this formalism is available at: https://github.com/Spangler/NCGR.

This study focuses on the repetitive outbursts of a subset of these transients to examine the feasibility of a periodicity. To avoid confusion, we will refer to this phenomenon as "repetitive outbursts" throughout this work.

Bipartite vertex splitting, a non-monotone graph transformation where a vertex is replaced by two interconnected vertices, serves as a fundamental operation in preprocessing strategies aimed at reducing the clique size during exact algorithms for Maximum Clique and Clique Coloring. While practical implementations exist, randomized experiments suggest that finding optimal splits—those yielding the smallest resulting clique size—remains computationally demanding for large graphs. This paper introduces a precise algorithm based on dynamic programming to identify the optimal bipartite splitting vertex for a given graph. Experimental outcomes indicate that the algorithm's running time aligns with the predicted theoretical complexity. These results also confirm the actual complexity of determining the optimal splitting vertex within a fixed part size for complete multipartite graphs. Furthermore, the study examines how such vertex splits impact the executable runtime of an existing exact algorithm, comparing scenarios with and without optimizing for the smallest feasible split. Finally, the research analyzes the effect of always selecting the complete multipartite graph as the splitting target. Extensive experiments were conducted using a 24-core server equipped with Intel Xeon E5-2650 v3 processors operating at 2.30GHz. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/RajivMehra99/Bipartite_Split. Evaluations of degraded service levels in SLAs have typically relied on CPU throttling, which is the least disruptive mechanism. However, existing assessments have always avoided combining different service degradation strategies. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a systematic framework for evaluating various CPU and non-CPU optimization techniques individually and, crucially, in diverse combinations. The results demonstrate that merging multiple non-CPU strategies yields significantly better outcomes than any single method alone. Furthermore, multiple configurations deliver performance nearly identical to aggressive CPU throttling—approximately 200% more efficient—without incurring the associated negative impacts. These findings suggest that SLAs can be fulfilled through approaches other than CPU throttling, thereby minimizing its use and the resulting drawbacks. To achieve this, cloud providers should adopt a multi-faceted degradation strategy rather than relying solely on CPU limits. Additional details, the open-source code, and trace data for HyperDegrade are accessible at https://github.com/shivam-989/HyperDegrade.

This paper introduces a tactical multi-agent collaboration framework designed to maximize the informational value of a team of autonomous vehicles operating on conventional networks with limited bandwidth. These vehicles possess both cognitive and sensory-limiting constraints. The proposed game theory-based approach formulates a multi-step tactic where a defending agent with limited attention selects an target from a list of potential options to engage, while a single attacking agent simultaneously decides which target to strike. Evaluated across multiple datasets, including the NYT and ASYNC datasets, our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of perplexity and $N$-gram metrics. Furthermore, the approach achieves a 2.1 improvement in BLEU scores compared to the best existing method on the NYT dataset and a 0.5 gain on the ASYNC dataset. Additionally, we demonstrated a 0.5 enhancement over prior work on measuring linguistic quality using a "semantic similarity" metric on the ASYNC dataset. The proposed framework offers a simple, highly effective solution for improving lexical quality to facilitate the creation of creative text, and it requires no manual annotation, making it particularly suitable for optimizing out-of-domain data. By combining neural and $N$-gram models, our method surpasses standalone neural approaches, particularly regarding lexical metrics, and even exceeds the linguistic quality of human-editing techniques on the NYT and ASYNC datasets. We utilize a simple, open-source "blob" model, which serves as a proxy for more complex General Circulation Models (GCMs), to explore how circulation evolves with increasing rotational speed, stellar irradiation, and gravity. Specifically, we investigate the combined effects of planetary rotation (coriolis force) and atmospheric heating (baroclinicity). Furthermore, we consider the impact of initial conditions, specifically the balance between centrifugal force and coriolis force. To organize these patterns, we introduce two potentially useful dynamical criteria: a baroclinic baross number and a coriolis number (analogous to the rydberg number). Additionally, we propose a new parameter, the initial centrifugal number (similar to the eckman number), as a metric for the strength of centrifugal forces. The expected patterns are validated through simulations within our blob model and by testing them against simple 2D and 3G extrapolar cross-sections of a known GCM. While our model is simpler than a GCM and lacks certain physical processes (discussed later), it offers the advantage of allowing precise control over initial and boundary conditions, as well as easy visualization of flow dynamics. Consequently, this simple model serves as an effective tool for exploring potential circulation patterns in extra-solar planetary atmospheres that may differ significantly from those found in terrestrial-like atmospheres. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spin distribution of TBHs after TDEs provides evidence against the existence of a universal lower threshold for Superradiance.
